doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Back to Chicago and the road to jail and illness
title: Tommy buys him a bass in Chicago, 1965
summary: A man Ware once helped buys him a $125 pawn-shop bass and pays his union dues.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: However, I went from one extreme to another, and I came back to New York in August of 1967, and while I was in Chicago -- now this was around '65, a young man I met up in New York in my dope fiend days, said I did him a favor one day. He was ill, and he spoke to me, and I had just copped, and said would I turn him on, and I said sure, come on. And I saw him in Chicago and he told me, he said, "You don't remember me, but you helped me one time" and he asked me where I was going and I told him, "Man, you ain't supposed to be in this kind of shape, so look, give me your phone number and I'll call you in a couple days."

So I give him Mama's phone number, and about a week later I'm over at the house and the phone rings and it's this cat Tommy, and he says, "Wilbur, I'm coming over. I'm gonna buy you a bass." And I said, "Oh, man ..." and he said, "No, I'm serious" and he said, "Get your coat ready" and we came on down. This was in November 1965, I believe. So we came down; he was on the South Side and he had to come up to 1898 Milwaukee Avenue -- that was my mother's apartment over there, and I get in the car and he says, "Where's the best place?" and I knew of a bass shop called Kagen and Kane, and I said, "Now man, wait

a minute, what you want from me? I said, 'You're not A.. I said, a horn or something like that.' What you want me to do; get a group together for you to manage it?' He said, 'No man, I just want you to have a weapon.' And to me, that was a beautiful statement; he said, 'You're a bass player and you should be out here playing, you know, and you're running around drinking this wine like you're crazy,' and he said, 'Come on.'

So we get down there and he says to pick one out, German and Czech so I'm checking out the basses, and I said to the salesman, 'How much do you want for that,' and he says $350 ... no, he says $450, and he says, 'Well, look, I'll give you $350 cash, and I say, 'Hold it, hold it,' you know, I say, 'This guy is nice enough to buy this and I know that we can go to the pawn shop and it wouldn't cost more than a hundred and some dollars.'

So I told him that and he said okay, you win. So I say, yeah, and we get in the car and we go out there to 47th and Prairie to Willis to a pawn shop Pond Shop, an outlet and they had a fiddle in there in an old [unintelligible] blonde case, and it didn't have no strings on it, naturally, and no cover, and I asked him how much he wanted for it, and he said, 'Oh, give me a hundred twenty-five' and Tommy said okay, and we went back downtown and got some strings, got a beautiful cover and a pick and the man fixed it up for me, and he said, 'Now let's go' -- and asked me about my union card, and I told him, and he went and shelled out $85 for that local 208.
